items.author: BitcoinNewsCom
items.context: @BitcoinNewsCom (266.446 seguidores), en inglés: Coinkite publicó un postmortem de 18 páginas sobre una falla de firmware de COLDCARD (marzo 2021 a julio 2026): las semillas se generaban con un RNG de software débil (~40 bits de entropía efectiva en Mk2/Mk3, ~72 bits en Mk4/Mk5/Q); se robaron 1.778,84 BTC sin acceso físico ni remoto a los dispositivos; actualizar el firmware no protege semillas ya comprometidas. Noticia fresca (~17 min), 2.522 vistas y solo 2 respuestas. Ángulo: custodia (entropía propia y migración de semilla).
items.suggested_text:
The detail that matters most here: the attackers never touched the devices, physically or remotely, and the coins left anyway. At ~40 bits of effective entropy a seed is within reach of a brute-force search, so the attacker didn't need the hardware, only the weak randomness it was born with.

That shifts the threat model. Isolation protects the signing; it says nothing about whether the seed was strong from day one. That's why user-supplied entropy, like dice rolls you can verify offline, has always been the quiet backstop: it doesn't depend on trusting a vendor's RNG or its audits, which here missed the flaw for five years.

And the last line deserves more attention than the headline: a firmware update doesn't fix a seed that was already weak. How many affected holders have updated and think they're done?
